prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement

The emerging task of Reference Audio-Visual Segmentation (Ref-AVS) demands a pixel-wise understanding of dynamic scenes where objects are identified via a combination of visual, auditory, and textual cues. Current approaches suffer from two primary limitations. First, dual-modality methods (Vision+Text or Vision+Audio) fail in complex scenarios where the third modality is required for disambiguation. Second, existing triple-modality frameworks struggle with **spatio-temporal consistency**; they often lose track of the target object over time or exhibit "target shift" due to a failure to maintain context across long video sequences. There is currently no effective method for adapting foundational video segmentation models (which typically rely on manual geometric prompts like points or boxes) to autonomously interpret these complex, multimodal semantic signals.

## Core Hypothesis

We hypothesize that the robustness of the Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) can be extended to Language-aided Audio-Visual Scenes (LAVS) by compressing disparate multimodal signals into a single, dynamic **learnable token**.

Our central intuition is that a "prompt" should not be a static embedding. Instead, the prompt token must behave as a dynamic agent that evolves alongside the video. By implementing a **Token Propagation** mechanism (forward knowledge transfer) combined with **Token Accumulation** (backward knowledge retention), we believe we can align semantic understanding with SAM2’s native video tracking capabilities. This will allow the model to maintain persistent focus on the referred object throughout a video without forgetting historical context or requiring manual intervention.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose a framework named **SAM2-LOVE**, designed to interface multimodal encoders with the SAM2 architecture. The approach consists of three distinct conceptual phases:

1.  **Multimodal Compression & Fusion:**
    We will utilize pre-trained encoders to extract features from video frames, audio clips, and text expressions. To unify these disjoint embedding spaces, we will introduce a **Multimodal Fusion Transformer**. This module will act as a compressor, digesting the raw features and outputting a single, high-density `[seg]` token. This token serves as the semantic anchor, representing the "instruction" for the segmentation model.

2.  **Dynamic Token Evolution (Propagation & Accumulation):**
    To address spatio-temporal inconsistency, the `[seg]` token will not remain static.
    *   **Token Propagation (Forward Flow):** The token will update iteratively. At each frame, the token from the previous step acts as input to the next, interacting with the current frame’s visual features while retaining the global audio/text context. This mimics a "tracking" behavior within the prompt itself.
    *   **Token Accumulation (Backward Flow):** To prevent the "dilution" of the original target information over long sequences (catastrophic forgetting), we will implement a history cache mechanism. A global representation token (`[his]`) will accumulate abstract features from all previous frames and be re-injected into the fusion process at every step. This ensures the prompt remains grounded in the history of the video.

3.  **Zero-Shot SAM2 Adaptation:**
    We aim to adapt SAM2 via a "prompt tuning" strategy rather than full fine-tuning. We will freeze the heavy image encoder and memory attention layers of SAM2. We will only train the fusion module and SAM2's prompt decoder/mask decoder.
    *   **Training Strategy:** We will align the learned `[seg]` token with the ground truth mask of the *first frame*. We rely on SAM2’s inherent ability to propagate masks (Video Object Segmentation) to handle the subsequent frames. This allows the system to learn multimodal alignment on a single frame and generalize to the entire video zero-shot.

## Expected Contribution

1.  **Unified Multimodal Framework:** We expect to provide the first framework that successfully integrates Audio, Vision, and Language into the foundational SAM2 architecture for pixel-level scene understanding.
2.  **Temporal Consistency Mechanism:** The proposed "Propagation and Accumulation" strategy offers a theoretical contribution to sequence modeling, defining a method to balance current-frame adaptation (forward flow) with historical context retention (backward flow).
3.  **Practical Generalization:** By leveraging the frozen backbone of SAM2, the approach aims to achieve high-quality segmentation and tracking in dynamic scenes without the need for massive retraining of the foundational visual model.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

*   **Dataset:** Ref-AVS Benchmark.
    *   **Content:** 4,000 videos with manual pixel-level annotations and 20,000 expressions.
    *   **Splits:** Training set (2,908 videos), Validation set (276 videos), Test set (818 videos).
    *   **Test Subsets:**
        *   *Seen:* 39 categories (same as training).
        *   *Unseen:* 13 additional categories (not in training).
        *   *Null:* Expressions referring to objects that do not exist or are not visible.
    *   **Modality Dimensions:** Audio, Vision, and Time (expressions reflect scenarios across these dimensions).
    *   **Video Statistics:** Average 1.72 objects per video, 48 audible object categories, 3 kinds of static objects.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Jaccard Index ($\mathcal{J}$):** Region similarity.
    *   **F-score ($\mathcal{F}$):** Contour accuracy.
    *   **Average ($\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$):** The average of Jaccard and F-score.
    *   **S-score (for Null split):** Square root of the ratio of the number of foreground pixels over the background pixels (lower is better for Null).

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   AVSBench (designed for AVS).
    *   AVSegFormer (designed for AVS).
    *   GAVS (designed for AVS).
    *   ReferFormer (designed for Ref-VOS).
    *   R2VOS (designed for Ref-VOS).
    *   EEMC (designed for Ref-AVS).
    *   *Note:* Missing modalities were provided to baselines to ensure fair comparison (e.g., adding text to AVS methods, audio to Ref-VOS methods).

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Encoders:**
        *   Audio: VGGish (frozen).
        *   Visual: ViT pre-trained on ImageNet (frozen).
        *   Text: DistilRoBERTa (frozen).
    *   **Model Initialization:** SAM2 initialized with `SAM2-Hiera-large` weights.
    *   **Fusion Transformer Architecture:** 6 stacked bi-directional transformer blocks, hidden dimension 1024, number of [seg] tokens set to 1.
    *   **Training Strategy:**
        *   Encoders and SAM2 Image Encoder/Memory Attention were frozen.
        *   Fusion transformer, [seg] token, SAM2 Prompt Encoder, Mask Decoder, and projection MLPs were trainable.
        *   SAM2 was exposed only to the first frame during training (using multimodal prompts), then generalized to the whole video during inference (zero-shot).
    *   **Hyperparameters:**
        *   Hardware: 2 NVIDIA A100 GPUs.
        *   Training Engine: DeepSpeed with ZeRO-2.
        *   Optimizer: AdamW.
        *   Learning Rate: 1e-4.
        *   Weight Decay: 0.
        *   Scheduler: WarmupDecayLR (100 warmup iterations).
        *   Batch Size: 8.
        *   Gradient Accumulation Step: 2.
    *   **Loss Function:** Combination of Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) and DICE loss. Weights: $\lambda_{bce} = 1.0$, $\lambda_{dice} = 1.0$.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Multimodal Dependencies:** We observed that previous dual-modality methods failed in specific scenarios: Text-Visual models struggled in silent scenes where audio cues were necessary, and Audio-Visual models failed to understand dynamic controls provided by text input.
*   **Fusion Strategy:** The fusion transformer successfully compressed multimodal cues (Audio, Vision, Text) into a learnable token ([seg]) containing both high semantics and positional information. This token accurately prompted SAM2 to segment targets.
*   **Visual Tracking:** SAM2 demonstrated strong zero-shot Video Object Segmentation (VOS) capabilities. It accurately tracked referred objects even when they disappeared and reappeared or interacted with similar objects.
*   **Comparison with SOTA (Visual Analysis):**
    *   In comparisons with EEMC, our method showed stronger spatio-temporal consistency across frames.
    *   Our method successfully tracked small referring targets in early frames where the baseline failed.
    *   Our method was more robust to changes in audible objects and complex expressions (e.g., distinguishing "shorter duration" vs. "the man"), whereas the baseline failed to interpret hidden meanings in expressions.
*   **Token Accumulation Effect:** The `[cls]` token accumulation strategy (appending global representations of previous frames) effectively prevented the `[seg]` token from forgetting historical information as it propagated, functioning as a backward knowledge transfer mechanism.
*   **Backbone Analysis:** RoBERTa and ViT backbones outperformed CLIP encoders. We attribute this to RoBERTa's stronger natural language understanding capabilities, which are crucial for processing complex expressions in LAVS that act as control signals (e.g., "the one making the most intense sound") rather than just category names.
*   **Token Count Analysis:** Increasing the number of `[seg]` tokens improved performance on Unseen splits (acting as registers for global info) but sacrificed performance on Seen splits. A single token provided a stronger inductive bias beneficial for Seen tasks.
*   **Limitation (Null Reference):** Our method exhibited a limitation in the "Null" split (0.23 score vs 0.007 for EEMC). The model struggled to reject user requirements for a null reference, often segmenting irrelevant regions instead of outputting nothing.

Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
The field of Language-aided Audio-Visual Scenes (LAVS) requires a model to perform pixel-wise scene understanding by continuously segmenting objects referred to by diverse multimodal cues (text and audio) within a video. While recent works such as Music-AVQA and AVQA address question-answering in this domain, they lack fine-grained, pixel-level understanding.

Current approaches to Reference Audio-Visual Segmentation (Ref-AVS) face two critical limitations. First, dual-modality methods (e.g., text-visual or audio-visual only) systematically fail when the object of interest requires a third modality for disambiguation (e.g., distinguishing a sounding object in a silent scene or understanding dynamic textual control over an audio source). Second, existing triple-modality methods (such as EEMC) struggle with spatio-temporal consistency; despite using memory caches, they often fail to track the target's position continuously, resulting in segmented area shifts over time. Furthermore, while the Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) provides powerful video tracking capabilities, it relies on manual visual prompts (points, boxes, masks) and lacks the inherent mechanism to interpret linguistic or acoustic control signals, restricting its application in LAVS.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose a novel framework, **SAM2-LOVE** (Segment Anything Model 2 in Language-aided audiO-Visual scEnes), to bridge the gap between multimodal inputs and SAM2's prompting mechanism.

Our core hypothesis is that we can compress information from three modalities (text, audio, and vision) into a single, learnable **segmentation token ([seg])**. By training a multimodal fusion module to align this token with the semantic space of SAM2, the token can serve as a "visual clue" to prompt SAM2 effectively. Furthermore, we hypothesize that implementing explicit **token propagation** (forward knowledge transfer) and **token accumulation** (backward knowledge transfer via history replay) strategies will enable the model to maintain robust spatio-temporal consistency across the entire video sequence, preventing the "forgetting" of historical context.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

### 1. Multimodal Representations and Alignment
We will utilize distinct, pre-trained encoders to extract representations for audio, video, and text. We will define the following extraction process:
*   **Audio:** We will use VGGish to encode audio clips into embeddings $F _ { A } \in R ^ { N \times d _ { A } }$, where $N$ represents the duration (and total video frames) and $d_A$ is the feature dimension.
*   **Visual:** We will employ a ViT pre-trained on ImageNet to encode sampled frames into $F _ { V } \in R ^ { N \times d _ { V } \times h \times w }$.
*   **Text:** We will utilize DistilRoBERTa to obtain textual representations $F _ { T } \in R ^ { P \times d _ { T } }$, where $P$ is the number of textual tokens.

To align these embeddings into a shared semantic space, we will project them using separate Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs). For any modality $Z \in \{ A , V , T \}$, the projection is defined as:
$$ \widehat { F } _ { Z } = L i n e a r ( \mathrm { R e L U } ( L i n e a r ( F _ { Z } ) ) ) $$

### 2. Multimodal Fusion Module
We will construct a multimodal fusion module based on a naive transformer encoder architecture consisting of $L$ stacked bi-directional transformer blocks. This module acts as the compressor for multimodal cues. It will process a sequence containing a learnable segmentation token `[seg]`.

The block operation for the $l$-th layer, where $z_{l-1}$ is the input sequence, is formulated as:
$$ \begin{array} { r l } & { z _ { l } ^ { \prime } = M S A ( L N ( z _ { l - 1 } ) ) + z _ { l - 1 } , \quad l = 1 . . . L } \\ & { z _ { l } = M L P ( L N ( z _ { l } ^ { \prime } ) ) + z _ { l } ^ { \prime } , \quad l = 1 . . . L } \end{array} $$
Here, MSA denotes Multi-Head Self-Attention and LN denotes LayerNorm.

### 3. Token Propagation Strategy (Forward Transfer)
To achieve spatio-temporal consistency, we will implement a self-propagation process for the `[seg]` token. For the $i$-th frame, we will construct a specific multimodal sequence $F _ { M } ^ { i }$ by prepending the current `[seg]` token to the concatenated modality features. We introduce fixed tokens `[aud]` and `[vis]` to demarcate modality boundaries:

$$ F _ { M } ^ { i } = C o n c a t ( [ [ s e g ] ; \widehat { F } _ { A } ; [ a u d ] ; \widehat { F } _ { T } ; [ v i s ] ; \widehat { F } _ { V } ^ { i } ] ) $$

We will extract the first element of the transformer output, $Q _ { i } = T r a n s f o r m e r ( F _ { M } ^ { i } )$, to serve as the updated `[seg]` token for the next step:
$$ [ s e g ] _ { updated } = Q _ { i } ^ { 0 } $$
This allows the token to evolve by aggregating information from the current visual frame and invariant audio/text features.

### 4. Token Accumulation Strategy (Backward Transfer)
To prevent the dilution of information from early frames during propagation, we will design a history accumulation mechanism. We will maintain a history sequence $[his]$ composed of the global representation tokens $[cls]$ from previous frames.

For the $i$-th frame, we define the history token sequence as:
$$ [ h i s ] ^ { i } = C o n c a t ( [ [ c l s ] ^ { 0 } ; [ c l s ] ^ { 1 } ; . . . ; [ c l s ] ^ { i } ] ) $$
where $[ c l s ] ^ { i }$ is the global representation of the $i$-th frame derived from the ViT. This sequence is concatenated into the input $F _ { M } ^ { i }$, enabling the current `[seg]` token to attend to global abstractions of all prior frames.

### 5. Integration with SAM2 and Training
We will integrate the fusion module with SAM2 by using the final `[seg]` token to prompt the SAM2 mask decoder.

**Training Strategy:**
*   **Frozen Components:** We will freeze the audio, video, and text encoders, as well as the SAM2 image encoder and memory attention modules.
*   **Trainable Components:** We will train the multimodal fusion transformer, the `[seg]` token, the projection MLPs, and the SAM2 prompt encoder and mask decoder.
*   **Process:** During training, we will expose SAM2 only to the first frame (supervised), while the fusion module accesses the full video sequence to generate the prompt. During inference, we will leverage SAM2's zero-shot Video Object Segmentation (VOS) capabilities to propagate the mask from the prompted frame to the rest of the video.

**Loss Function:**
We will define the total supervised mask loss $\mathcal { L } _ { m a s k }$ as a combination of per-pixel Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) and DICE loss:
$$ \mathcal { L } _ { m a s k } = \lambda _ { b c e } \mathbf { B } \mathbf { C } \mathbf { E } ( \hat { M } , M ) + \lambda _ { d i c e } \mathbf { D } \mathbf { I } \mathbf { C } \mathbf { E } ( \hat { M } , M ) $$
where $\hat { M }$ is the mask prediction for the frame, $M$ is the ground truth label, and $\lambda _ { b c e }$, $\lambda _ { d i c e }$ are the corresponding loss weights.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Framework Innovation:** We expect to provide the first framework that effectively prompts SAM2 using complex multimodal signals (Audio-Visual-Language) for pixel-wise scene understanding, eliminating the need for manual visual prompts in LAVS.
2.  **Spatio-Temporal Consistency:** Through our proposed Token Propagation (forward flow) and Token Accumulation (backward flow) strategies, we anticipate solving the target shift issue prevalent in existing methods by maintaining a unified perspective of knowledge transfer.
3.  **Modular Efficiency:** By designing a mechanism that aligns diverse modalities into a single token while freezing the majority of the SAM2 backbone, we expect to achieve State-of-the-Art performance with efficient training requirements.

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.

Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
